metadata.title: Nested Logarithms and Inverse-Function Chains
metadata.description: Evaluate nested logarithms from the inside outward and reverse nested equations while checking every intermediate domain.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop definitions and laws step by step, explain why each transformation is valid, show intermediate calculations and checks, and use targeted practice with changed-value remedial retries.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 10 “Logarithms,” printed pages 297–307. Approved scope: Evaluate nested expressions such as log_a(log_b(log_c x)) by working from the innermost function outward, converting each known logarithm to its defining exponential equation. Solve nested-log equations by reversing the chain in the correct order. Verify every intermediate argument is positive and each base valid; do not assume a nested expression exists just because its innermost logarithm does. Use patterns from the chapter's nested objective questions while creating fresh values.

content.text: Welcome to Nested Logarithms and Inverse-Function Chains. Evaluate nested logarithms from the inside outward and reverse nested equations while checking every intermediate domain.

In a nested expression, the innermost logarithm is evaluated first. For log_2(log_3(81)), start with log_3(81)=4, then evaluate log_2(4)=2. The outer logarithm cannot be attempted until its argument is known.
Every outer argument must be positive. In log_2(log_3(x)), the condition is not merely x>0: the inner value log_3(x) must itself be greater than 0, which for base 3 means x>1.
Nested equations can be reversed one layer at a time. If log_2(log_3(x))=2, then the outer equality gives log_3(x)=2^2=4; the inner equality gives x=3^4=81.
The order of reversal matters. Given log_a(log_b(x))=c, first exponentiate with base a to recover log_b(x)=a^c, then exponentiate with base b to recover x=b^(a^c).

A chain may include power functions between logs. For example log_2((log_3 x)^2) requires (log_3 x)^2>0, and solving the equation may produce two algebraic signs for log_3 x. Test which signs are allowed by the original outer argument.
Do not replace log_a(log_b x) with log_(ab)(x). Nested functions are composition, not multiplication of bases. Evaluate in order or translate each equality through its definition.
Example: solve log_3(log_2 x)=2. The outer equation gives log_2 x=3^2=9; the inner gives x=2^9=512. Check: log_2(512)=9 and log_3(9)=2.

Example: evaluate log_2(log_3(log_2 256)). Inner to outer: log_2(256)=8, log_3(8) remains an exact logarithm not an integer, and the outer log_2 requires this value to be positive. The expression is defined, but there is no simple integer evaluation. Do not invent one.
When each nested layer is designed to return a recognizable power, simplify exact values: log_2(log_3(log_2 512)) gives log_2(log_3 9)=log_2(2)=1.

The source includes nested questions built from logs of powers and logs of small integers. Their pattern is inverse cancellation: an inner logarithm simplifies a power, then the next layer acts on the result.

Check nested domains from the outside inward as well as evaluating inside outward. Every layer’s output must be positive when it is used as the next argument, and every base must remain positive and different from 1.
If the innermost equation yields x as a power, preserve exact form. For example x=5^6 is clearer and exact; write 15625 only if a numerical value helps the learner check.

Nested equations sometimes produce a candidate whose inner log is zero or negative, which makes the next log invalid. Such a candidate must be rejected even if it solves an algebraically transformed equation.
Use a small table with columns “layer,” “known value,” and “inverse step” when several logs are nested. This prevents reversing in the wrong order.
The practice asks for each intermediate value or domain condition explicitly. State the inner result first, then apply the outer inverse, and check by rebuilding the original chain.

A three-layer example shows the order clearly: log_2(log_3(log_2(512))). First log_2(512)=9; then log_3(9)=2; finally log_2(2)=1. Write each intermediate result before moving outward to avoid applying a base to the wrong layer.

Nested domains can be stricter than the innermost domain. For log_2(log_3(x)), the inner logarithm exists for x>0, but the outer one also requires log_3(x)>0. Because base 3 is greater than 1, that reduces the complete domain to x>1.

When the inner base lies between 0 and 1, reverse the sign test. For log_2(log_(1/3)(x)), the outer argument needs log_(1/3)(x)>0, which occurs for 0<x<1. The complete domain is a bounded interval, not simply x>1.

Solving by reversal is safest when written as two equations. If log_a(log_b(x))=c, first set log_b(x)=a^c. Then set x=b^(a^c). Finally check that the inner logarithm value a^c is positive and that all bases are allowed.

If an outer log is defined, its argument cannot be zero even when the inner log itself is valid. For instance, log_2(log_3(1)) is not real: log_3(1)=0, and zero is not a permitted argument for the outer logarithm.
